speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head R of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through the measures, many of which were introduced as Bills on Certificates of Urgency, these businesses were able to obtain relief that allowed them to conserve on cashflow and be protected from legal action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Like with most pieces of legislation, these are dry names but for matters vital to our economic and personal lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They mean the difference between a state of uncertainty and precariousness, and one of dignity and purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have made a difference for large groups of people – not just owners of small businesses, but the many workers employed in these businesses and companies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For parents, they mean the difference between paying attention to their children's education and future, instead of worrying about food on the table; for tenants, rental relief meant they could focus on rethinking their business and relying on their landlords as trusted partners.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For those who need to wind up their business, through the heartache and emotional difficulty of letting go a dream, there is the assurance of simplicity and speed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are not the subjects of headlines, but they are common sense writ hard into law – due to the pandemic, circumstances have changed, and not due to the fault of any party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While contracts are ordinarily written as a means to hold people fast to their promises, these COVID-19 legislative measures allow a common understanding and the general principles for re-negotiation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These require parties to work a basis of mutual trust in mutual gains, rather than a position that one party is trying to gain advantage over the other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The COVID-19 legislation is an extraordinary effort to make law bend to the realities, and to compensate for exogenous factors such as misfortune, bad luck and in this case, a global pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Law, in a memorable speech made last year in this House, informed how within just nine days, his Ministry, with the help of Government agencies, the hon Attorney-General and his officers from the Attorney-General's Chambers and private sector professionals and lawyers, came together, conceptualised the support framework and drafted the legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: People in the know will acknowledge the superb quality of the legislation which had to be drafted from scratch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The team members behind the legislation, no doubt, made personal sacrifices so that Singaporeans facing an almost certain financial ruin and uncertainty will get a reprieve instead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With almost a year has past, since the implementation of the first COVID-19 legislation, this may be an opportune time to recount the efficacy of and the feedback received on these measures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Have they worked as the Minister had anticipated?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we are not out of the woods yet from the economic effects of the pandemic, what further legislative measures can we anticipate in the future?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, is it time that we think of having a framework legislation that can be employed swiftly when the next crisis hits us?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, please allow me to share a situation that happened recently in Texas, US as reported in a New York Times article dated 20 February 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members may know, a winter storm knocked off Texas power grid and froze natural gas production.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, electricity prices, which was tied to wholesale prices and market-driven, spiked astronomically.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some Texans had to pay up to 70 times what they usually pay for the utilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must ensure that we have legislative levers to be able to move swiftly to prevent such instances from happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I look forward to the hon Ministers' responses to my queries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister responded then stating that the matter is under review by the relevant agencies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Even for allowing for an increase in the percentage in the three years plus that has passed, by international standards, this is rather low.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The trouble, anxiety and financial difficulties caused by the lack of a will, especially when the breadwinner dies, is real.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The low numbers present an opportunity for us though to modernise the processes spelt out in the Wills Act enacted 183 years ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the same time, the probate and administration processes can be updated to make it fuss-free for applicants by leveraging on the Government's archive of key documents, maybe even in lieu of court applications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I will be grateful if the hon Minister please provide an update on the efforts to modernise and simplify the probate and administration processes by leveraging on IT.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The response was timely, effective and I commend it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This included legislation to assist tenants in the payment of rental.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, small landlords need to be helped too because the rental relief given to tenants can be overly onerous on them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While many landlords have diversified income, many rely heavily on the rental yield as retirement income.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To be subject to the rental relief, an additional rental relief scheme places a heavy burden on landlords running SMEs who do not have the same capacity as larger companies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The pandemic has shown us our common humanity and has not differentiated between the affluent and the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, it has certainly placed vulnerable people in an even more precarious situation, and often they do not have the same means to let their voice be heard in Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How does MinLaw intend to provide more support and create more channels for the vulnerable to have access to justice?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not have too high a barrier to entry to allow anyone equal access to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, neither must we become overzealous about providing funding for the defendant to criminal cases such that the process would be abused.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Everyone should have access to the courts to bring rightful claims and to properly defend themselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, criminal legal aid is available through the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) administered by the Law Society Pro Bono Services (LSPBS), which is co-funded by MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The legal fraternity has been supportive of this scheme, with many volunteer lawyers participating actively.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Various measures had been rolled out in the past year to assist businesses with their legal troubles amidst the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: However, individuals who may have lost their jobs or had their livelihoods affected by the pandemic will also need help with legal representation if they inadvertently fall afoul of the law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, the crises brought on by COVID-19 has contributed to significant worldwide increases in domestic violence cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many studies have highlighted the acute vulnerabilities particularly faced by single mothers, foreign domestic workers and foreign spouses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The most vulnerable are children, who do not have the knowledge and means to escape from the clutches of their abusers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The situation is much more complex when the perpetrators are the care-givers and the cases go unreported.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Domestic violence goes beyond the family but also include intimate partner violence and violence against other vulnerable groups like foreign domestic workers and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A research study on intimate partner violence and the Global Financial Crisis in the United States found that unemployment and economic hardship were related to abusive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How does MinLaw intend to provide more support for enhancing access to justice for vulnerable groups?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, are there any plans to enhance current protection for elderly persons, persons with mental or physical disabilities, or young children, especially in situations where the perpetrator was the primary care-giver?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After all, violence is violence, whether inflicted on a spouse, boyfriend or girlfriend or a partner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the interim, what is being done to beef up the Enhanced Criminal Legal Aid Scheme to increase the availability of criminal legal aid to the economically vulnerable applicants.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I have met Clementi residents who have serious medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, this means having to move in with family members.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of my residents is ill – visually impaired, on dialysis.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because of his condition, he moved in with a family member, for care-giving support.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But because of this, he does not qualify for legal aid.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But I am sure there are other families in Singapore facing the same dilemma.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They should not have to choose between having a family member as care-giver staying together and falling on the wrong side of the means test assessment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our agencies mean well and I hope we can continue finding ways to support families in such challenging unfortunate situations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, often, access to justice is not something people think about until they are in need of a just and timely legal outcome.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the iLab Chatbot or the My Legacy website in beta testing phase.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, digital solutions may not be useful for elderly or less tech-savvy Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Planning for end-of-life issues can be very sensitive.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, I would first like to declare that I am the Co-Chairperson of the Law Society Pro Bono Services’ Community Legal Clinics Committee.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong in his foreword for the fourth publication of the Singapore Association of Women Lawyer (SAWL)’s "You & the Law" said: "It is said that a little knowledge is a dangerous thing.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, in the case of the law, a little knowledge of one’s rights, duties and responsibilities goes some way to empower him or her a more confident person in his or her daily life." I fully agree with his honour.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The increase in scam cases and the helplessness faced by individuals when he or she losses their loved ones unexpectedly, made me realise that upstream education is always important.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, organisations such as SAWL and the Law Society of Singapore have respectively published books, written in plain language, for members of the public on various topics of Singapore law relevant to everyday life, imparting easy-to-understand legal knowledge and information into the hands of every man in the street.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Separately, we have also seen agencies such as the Office of the Public Guardian providing step-by-step guide on their website to enable Singaporeans have a better understanding on the importance of doing Lasting Power of Attorney.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, this involves either a neighbour who makes too much noise in the middle of the night or a neighbour who places his personal plants, bicycles, beyond the common shared space in the corridor.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Sometimes, the quarrel arose over minute matters, which then escalate into vulgar language being used or thrown at each other.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I have also come across cases involving hoarders who accumulate junk in the flat and, in the process, block the common area causing fire hazard to the neighbours.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is also a hygiene issue as there may be cockroaches and rats that would come through the house.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Frequently, we ask HDB staff, we ask Town Council staff and sometimes even Grassroots leaders to help by mediating between the involved parties.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But the dispute between neighbours are very difficult to resolve.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many of them refuse to attend mediation at the Community Mediation Centre.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The final option is to refer parties to the Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal or CDRT.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But from feedback, many residents are reluctant to go that step.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many do not think that mediation would solve their dispute.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They also think that going to the Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal would not solve their dispute.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They continue to suffer in silence and the resentment festers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And sometimes, even after resolving the matter at the Tribunal, the problem does not go away.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The hurt and resentment remains as egos are hurt.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is especially for cases where the neighbour can be very unreasonable, or what sometimes, the newspaper refers to as "neighbours from hell".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After a case is resolved, is there any tracking of the case?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am concerned that sometimes, the CDRT may consider a case as closed when the Tribunal makes an Order.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And when I visit them as Minister of Parliament, they would each bring their source of complaints to me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So would an order, would a mandatory order for counselling help mitigate the tension between the parties?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This may be similar to a family court order for parties to go for counselling before a Police Protection Order (PPO) application.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has the specialist court been set up for the protection from harassment?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Neighbour disputes are some of the most thorny issues in public housing estates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Residents often contact the police, HDB, town councils or the Ministers of Parliament to seek assistance.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Avenues like the Community Mediation Centre (CMC), or Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal (CDRT), are available, but many residents seem less keen on using them, because of perceived administrative hurdles or perceived ineffectiveness.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can there be a more streamlined, efficient and effective process available to residents at the first instance?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The CMC could be that avenue, but it first needs to be given more resources and more teeth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can also help boost their authority in the eyes of the disputing parties.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And fourth, the Government should publicise the CMC more, so residents know that they can contact the CMC before they call the police or HDB to settle their disputes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I believe that if these proposals can be implemented, the CMC will provide a more streamlined avenue for residents to seek a resolution to their disputes and relieve the burden of mediating these neighbour disputes on agencies like the Police.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: First cut is on the updates on the CDRT.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Since the set up of the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal, I wish to ask the Ministry of Law how many cases have been filed, how many heard, how many cases mediated and how many resolved annually.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Also, what actions, if any, has the courts or complainants taken when offending parties after the tribunal order still continue to perpetrate and breach the order.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I also ask the Ministry of Law to elucidate on how the CDRT can better ensure the efficient and effective resolution of CDRT complaints as there are more situations of work from home and resulting in more neighbourly disputes and some of these disputes cannot be resolved via the voluntary mediation via Community Mediation and so on, and whether such mediation can be made compulsory.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Since coming into force in November 2014, can Ministry of Law provide an update on the number of cases filed and mediated?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Among all the POHA cases filed, what is the breakdown on the types of those involving community or neighbours, how many are online harassment, how many are sexual harassment and how many are workplace harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: If not already monitored, can I request that the figures be closely monitored and published regularly so that we know the exact magnitude of the various forms of harassment including the extent of workplace harassment and bullying as well as the prevalence of sexual harassment in workplaces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I also ask the Ministry of Law to elucidate on the POHA Court and how this court can better ensure the efficient and effective resolution of harassment complaints.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: My third and final cut, enforcement and publication of Employment Claims Tribunal Judgment and Orders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The Employment Claims Tribunal now has jurisdiction to adjudicate both salary-related disputes as well as wrongful dismissal claims, making it more convenient for parties to resolve employment disputes via a single forum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, an Employment Claims Tribunal judgment that is not satisfied would still need to be enforced in the same manner as an Order made by a District Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This would involve detailed processes set out in the Rules of Court pertaining to the filing of relevant forms, documents as well as the payment of court fees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: A worker who has successfully obtained a judgment may thus still be subject to a protracted enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Workers’ lack of knowledge of the workings of our courts system exacerbates this problem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There is thus a need to simplify and expedite the enforcement mechanism to facilitate workers’ recovery of monies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: With the Employment Claims Tribunal having jurisdiction to adjudicate both salary-related disputes as well as wrongful dismissal claims, it now hears more cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Having a deeper understanding of the rulings of the Employment Claims Tribunal would benefit not just practitioners and lawyers, but claimants and respondents too, when they have to present their respective cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Past decisions of the Employment Claims Tribunal would be extremely useful as a source of reference and precedence and should thus be made available.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: For a start, I would like to suggest that the more landmark and instructive judgments can be selectively published for the benefit of all.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, law firms have generally been quite slow to adopt technology, preferring to rely on traditional means of work and a manpower heavy modus operandi.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Separately, Sir, with Singapore's stellar reputation as a legal hub, it would be prudent for us to encourage our law firms to expand overseas.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Our larger local firms like Allen & Gledhill and Rajah & Tann, already have a well-established presence overseas.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: Our SME law firms should also be looking at expanding especially because they are located in an international arbitration and mediation hub.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In particular, our law firm SMEs should look at least in the first instance, at doing work in our region.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: However, given that travel restrictions due to COVID-19 are likely to affect these programmes, which typically saw Singapore lawyers making overseas trips, we may have to find new ways to support our firms' internationalisation aspirations and activities.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas
text: In this regard, I would like to ask the Minister for Law, how does the Ministry of Law intend to support law firms to internationalise and capture more work from the region?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Twenty-twenty was a challenging year for many and the legal sector was not spared the effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, when the circuit breaker was implemented, lawyers had to quickly adjust and adapt to work from home, make alternative arrangements to meet and communicate with clients, and then to have court sessions online.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The sector had to quickly adapt and accelerate the adoption of technology.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The development of technology in legal practice has been in the horizons for some time now, but the pandemic obviously gave a hard nudge to the sector and hastened the progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This did not just mean that lawyers had to learn new skills to manage their practice with new technology.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It also meant that they had to contend with potential competition, with the advent of artificial intelligence and the development of online platforms for lay persons, which inevitably meant less dependence on lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To be clear, I am not suggesting that we should not allow for these developments just so as to preserve the lawyers' relevance in society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe these advancements are important and necessary and we should always look at platforms and opportunities to make the law accessible to the public.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, lawyers from small- and medium-sized firms may face more challenges than others in pivoting and developing their practice into one that is relevant to the times and to seize opportunities in areas of growth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe there are two areas which the Ministry could look into.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One, the support for adoption of technology and two, training and development programmes that could empower lawyers from these films by building substantive knowledge on different fields where there is potential growth.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the opening of legal year 2021, the president of the Law Society of Singapore, Senior Counsel Mr Gregory Vijayendran, made reference to the dialogue with the Ministry of Law on a technology platform in a pipeline and a promising initiative of effectively Plug and Play Technology Solutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could we enhance our support for technology adoption?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some of the adoption may require customization to suit the needs of the firm.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may take the lawyers some time to learn the platforms or standard solutions and some more time to build a customised solution for their set-up.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Lawyers from small- and medium-sized firms may not have IT staff or teams to support them with this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, would there be sustainable funding or grants to support these firms with the developments?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the second area, could we enhance the platforms available to the lawyers from the small- and medium-sized firms to give them more exposure to new and developing fields of work?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from exposure, could there also be opportunities for lawyers from these firms to develop specialisation and deep knowledge for a particular field so that they could potentially develop a boutique practice in a specific area of growth?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, lawyers are required to accumulate continuing professional development points and attend various training sessions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, these sessions may not be sufficient to develop specialised skills.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be helpful if the lawyers could be supported with a training and development programme that could help them pivot and succeed in a new and growing field.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 may just be the catalyst of change for our legal profession.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Due to COVID-19, legal courts have undergone speedy digitisation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last week, I just finished an international court trial with a presiding judge in London.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the new changes and challenges faced by the legal profession today, how is the Ministry of Law equipping practitioners, firms and law students for the future?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Separately, Singapore Academy of Law’s Future Law Innovation Programme called FLIP, had aimed to drive innovation and adoption of new technology amongst law firms in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This shows that mediation is an effective dispute resolution mechanism and, it is with little wonder, that it has grown more popular over time, especially in commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is less contentious and, with an effective and experienced mediator, could even help previously warring parties find a way to collaborate commercially again, post-settlement.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, from a business perspective, is a very attractive proposition.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are also many reputable international organisations and institutions such as the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), World Intellectual Property Organization Arbitration and Mediation Center (WIPO AMC) and the International Centre for Dispute Resolution-American Arbitration Association (ICDR-AAA), which have set up offices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These organisations and institutions will go a long way to complement our position as a dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Through this journey, sir, we have also developed world-class infrastructure to facilitate conducting dispute resolution in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Maxwell Chambers, launched in 2010, expanded to the adjacent Maxwell Chambers Suites in 2019, has tripled in size and now houses international dispute resolution institutions and practices with state-of-the-art hearing facilities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It therefore appears that Singapore is well placed to capitalise on these developments and resources.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as this House is aware, the current COVID-19 pandemic has forced many countries around the world to impose strict travel restrictions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This could potentially derail Singapore's efforts in positioning itself as a leading international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share with this House the Ministry's larger strategic plans, especially in light of international COVID-19 travel restrictions, so as to continue to promote Singapore as a leading global dispute resolution hub to resolve international cross-border commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has forged a hard-earned reputation of being one of the most preferred dispute resolution centres in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Over the years, the Ministry of Law has introduced a slew of measures to improve her dispute resolution framework.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is an old treaty that came into being in 1965.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Its purpose is simple: to offer a reliable and efficient means of serving court documents from parties living, operating or based in another country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The convention applies to service of process in civil and commercial matters but not criminal matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Signing up for the Hague Service Convention will allow for service of judicial documents in civil matters abroad without the need to invoke time consuming and uncertain consular processes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would be grateful for the hon Minister's response to my suggestion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: At this stage, I should declare that I am a lawyer who practises intellectual property law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When the pandemic was at its worst in Singapore and we needed temporary buildings to house our essential foreign workers, I must state on record that SLA did excellent in converting under-utilised buildings into temporary dormitories.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I had the pleasure of working together with SLA officers and officers from related agencies on the conversion of the old Nexus International School in Ulu Pandan into a temporary dormitory.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is the type of innovation that we should continue to promote and prompt agencies to maximise their venues of under-utilised plots land in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to consistently review our usage of land and see how we can renew and optimise our land resources, whether it is for housing, sports and recreational activities or commercial and industrial purposes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, the Ministry of Law has already taken many steps in its digitisation journey.
Head R (cont) –   , (proc text)]  .

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In terms of challenges, we look at how our legal framework can continue to achieve fairness, remain accessible to all, achieve justice in a changing world and ensure that these legal services remain accessible, available, including to the most vulnerable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we also face opportunities, on how we can reposition, re-envision and strengthen our legal industry – to ride on opportunities arising from technology, to contribute to new areas of industrial growth, and ultimately, to contribute to Singapore's strong and vibrant economic growth.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our response will determine whether we will be able to preserve the trust and international reputation, that we have worked so hard to gain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will share some details on how we intend to achieve this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Gerald Giam and Mr Patrick Tay asked about community disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an issue that is very much on our minds, and I think on the minds of many Members in this House.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Particularly perhaps, in the past year, where people have been working from home; staying at home a lot more during the circuit breaker period, where there has been a reported rise in neighbourly nuisance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: By and large, CDRT proceedings are designed to be quick and straightforward.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, the management of disputes between neighbours is not as straightforward.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is a delicate and often a challenging area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And while we endeavour to resolve disputes amicably between the disputing parties, neighbours can sometimes refuse to communicate, or sometimes, refuse to come together, or to compromise, and this can then lead to a breakdown in relationships.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as Mr Lim points out, which we agree, an adjudication of rights in this context may solve that legal problem, but it does not solve the longer lasting dispute between the parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members have pointed out, we have put in place several avenues for parties to work through their disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Community mediation is one – it is affordable, and we have seen that it is effective when both parties approach it in the right spirit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we would like to assure Mr Giam that CMC's mediators are trained, they are accredited and they are fully equipped with a specific skillset to handle community disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as the numbers have shown, they have been successful.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The challenge, however, is getting parties to mediation, because mediation is largely voluntary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are also many parties who refuse to turn up for mediation, and that can arise from any number of different reasons peculiar to the case.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is not healthy for the neighbourly relationship in the longer term and my Ministry acknowledges that we can look at how we can improve the take-up rate of mediation, perhaps, make it compulsory, and these are areas we are studying seriously.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I will explain some details in a moment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Lim points out in his speech, for parties to commence CDRT proceedings – that is another option that is available.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But there are also limits to what courts in the adjudicatory process can do.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The courts are ultimately the arbiters of who is legally right and legally wrong, and this is a binary zero-sum game.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are not structured to help parties mend their relationships nor can they supervise or monitor how parties behave after the specific proceedings end.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we are mindful of the above limitations and of the need to address these community disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is going to be a complex study that involves several Ministries, but I would just quickly, broadly outline in this House the three areas that the committee is looking at.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, it will look at how neighbourly disputes can be better managed and resolved up front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When disagreements arise, we need to quickly identify and address the root cause of the issues.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This helps to preserve the goodwill before it festers and progressively tapers down.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And also, in this context, community leaders can play a big role.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also looking to measures to increase the take-up of community mediation, as I have mentioned, including increasing the awareness of the benefits of mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will consider Mr Tay, Mr Giam and Mr Lim's suggestion on compulsory mediation and counselling; and Mr Giam might know that the product of a successful mediation is often a mediated agreement, which we have the legal framework to enforce as a binding arrangement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also explore Mr Lim's suggestion to continue tracking a case even after it has been disposed of by the CDRT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CDRT should continue to be the avenue of last resort, but as Members know it is often still necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we are considering several refinements to better address these disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, we are considering if CDRT can make interim orders, especially in cases of severe and continuing nuisance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also aware that some claimants can find it difficult to gather evidence to support their claims, and this is even though the CDRT is not bound strictly by the rules of evidence and the proceedings are judge-led.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will look at whether clarifications are needed in the legislation to ensure that parties do not find CDRT proceedings unreasonably and unnecessarily onerous.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In some cases, respondents have, however, wilfully refused to comply with the CDRT's orders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In one egregious case, the respondent started to create a different type of nuisance not covered by the CDRT order, presumably to spite the claimant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will look at how these gaps can be closed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If a party does not comply with the CDRT order, the CDRT may issue a special direction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Non-compliance with a Special Direction is a criminal offence, and can result in a court order that excludes the offending party from his or her place of residence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also look at whether the current measures are sufficient to protect our communities from anti-social and nuisance behaviour.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Of these, 135, or more than one in five, were ordered to undergo mediation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On average, since 2018, the CDRT has disposed of slightly over 100 cases annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The majority of cases are resolved within six months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The remainder, within 12 months, with a small handful outside of 12 months.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are studying the three areas above that I have outlined, carefully, and will introduce reforms to strengthen our management of community disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These will be announced when the study is concluded.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Notwithstanding what I have said, whilst we can introduce more regulations and enhanced measures, ultimately, at the end of the day, it is fundamental for neighbours to maintain a culture of open communication, mutual respect and understanding.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And to the extent possible, may I also ask that Members refer and encourage parties them to attend mediation, given that the mediators are well-trained and the numbers show that CMC has proven successful in resolving these disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: By and large, mediation has a far more sustainable, longer term, long lasting impact in maintaining the relationship between two neighbours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Tay and Mr Lim asked about the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Derrick Goh also touched on harmful online speech, in his cut filed with the MHA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, dealing with the number of cases filed with POHA to date.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes application by victims of sexual and workplace harassment, online harassment, as well as harassment by neighbours.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Data based on types of harassment are currently not available, but the State Courts are looking into enhancing the case management system to capture and track such data.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Three hundred and forty-eight POs were granted, of which more than half were granted with the consent of both parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This suggests that a good number of cases were, after the process had started, were resolved amicably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The few remaining applications were either withdrawn, dismissed or struck off or remain pending resolution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2019, Members may recall that we amended POHA, created new offences such as doxxing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also enhanced the suite of tools available, for example, having new remedies for victims of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This year, the dedicated Protection from Harassment Courts will begin operation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was designed with the end-user in mind.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Volunteers will also be on hand to help victims navigate the process, and judges will be specially trained to deal with harassment matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The POHA Court will adopt simplified procedures and expedited timelines for certain types of applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we will continue to monitor the effectiveness of the 2019 amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will provide a more holistic assessment after the POHA Court has been in operation for some time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These should also address Mr Derrick Goh's earlier questions to MHA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, let me turn to Mr Pillai's suggestions to modernise and simplify the probate processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think Ms Nadia Samdin also raised similar questions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Courts are working on an online application for straightforward probate matters for individuals to use directly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, something that individuals can use on their own as lay persons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will be linked to Government agencies' database so that relevant information can be retrieved, without users having to provide additional information or fill up any more documents than might be necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Safeguards, however, will have to continue to be placed because for probate matters, we do have to ensure the integrity of the process, as well as look after the interests of the beneficiaries.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Vikram Nair has filed cuts about our efforts to manage the moneylending sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We monitor the borrowing trends and developments very closely.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have previously adjusted our regulatory framework to ensure safe access to credit for vulnerable borrowers and will continue to do so as may be necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will recall that in July 2019, we introduced a comprehensive suite of measures to stem the increase in moneylending activities targeting foreigners, in particular, foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To help borrowers affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, we worked with Credit Association of Singapore (CAS) to encourage licensed moneylenders to adopt various measures to assist borrowers including debt restructuring and also debt consolidation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have received feedback from affected borrowers that these efforts by CAS and licensees have been helpful and we are grateful to CAS' cooperation with us on this front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, let me turn to effective access to justice which a number of Members – Mr de Souza, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Joshua Thomas, Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Leong Mun Wai – have spoken about enhancing legal assistance for the vulnerable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There have been observations that the COVID-19 pandemic has worsened what some might term the "justice gap".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The disruptions caused by the pandemic has raised demand for legal resolutions and also has affected the industry unequally.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, those disruptions may impact the vulnerable, as I have said, disproportionately – and they are the same ones who often find it difficult to access legal services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This backdrop and the recent experience has deepened my Ministry's resolve to enhance access to justice for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Legal Aid Bureau, or LAB, launched iLAB in February 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a free legal chatbot that provides customised legal information on key topics such as divorce, personal protection orders, custody and guardianship, and maintenance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are issues that most lay persons commonly seek assistance on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: During the height of the pandemic, the chatbot was enhanced to provide answers to commonly asked legal queries that arose from the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: LAB revamped its Applicant Portal in February 2020, allowing applicants to make their applications, to do their means testing, and to give their instructions, all online.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Through this process enhancements, processing time was also shortened by at about two weeks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will push ahead with our efforts to make legal information and advice more accessible in 2021.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: LAB will add more topics to the iLAB chatbot.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will also expand its partnerships with social agencies to offer legal advice via video-conferencing and at various community touchpoints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, to put it out in the community, on the ground through partners such as including Our Tampines Hub, Family Service Centres, essentially to make services more accessible directly to vulnerable applicants, as Ms Samdin has suggested.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw is also working with the Law Society Pro Bono Services, or LSPBS, to develop a one-stop legal information portal – which Ms Hany Soh asked about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This online portal will provide members of the public with clear and easily understandable information on common legal topics.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will also provide information as to the various sources of legal assistance available.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng spoke about increasing flexibility in means testing to assist legal aid applicants with exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we have built in a set of rules, so that officers can, within these rules, exercise discretion in assessing an application.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, if an applicant has severe disability and/or illness, and/or is 60 years old or above, the means test assessment can exclude some of the applicant's savings in computing their eligibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond this, we have established an independent Means Test Panel, which reviews cases that do not satisfy the means criteria but are unable otherwise to afford basic legal services due to exceptional circumstances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Panel has done so for a few cases and will continue to exercise this discretion, judiciously, where the case merits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In Dr Tan's case, I would invite him to let us have the details of that specific case for our review and see how we can assist.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In a survey conducted by my Ministry in late 2020, three in four respondents agreed that legal aid is accessible to those in need.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, let me speak about enhancements to criminal legal aid which Mr de Souza and Mr Leong spoke about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Enhanced CLAS receives an average of 2,400 applications annually – all of whom receive some basic legal advice.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More than half, or 1,400 applicants per year on average are supported under CLAS and received full legal representation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is more than three times the number of applicants who had benefited from full legal representation prior to Enhanced CLAS in 2015.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CLAS currently covers 17 Acts – these account for about 70% of non-capital criminal charges filed in the State Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are carefully studying the experiences of other countries to avoid the problems they have encountered, such as abuses of legal aid by wealthy defendants and its corresponding impact on the legal fraternity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will consider both the coverage and the measures we should adopt to ensure that we have a sustainable criminal legal aid model.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the meantime, we will continue to make improvements to legal assistance for accused persons under CLAS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But the changes will simplify the application process and also reduce the paperwork for applicants, compared to the current process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, LSPBS introduced and launched a new online application process for criminal legal aid which provides applicants with detailed, step-by-step guidance on how to apply online, should they seek to do that.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, from the own portals and in person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: LSPBS has also established a referral protocol with the Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Courts can refer accused persons who need legal assistance but who are unable themselves to apply online, directly to LSPBS, to ensure that help is available even for those who are less digitally savvy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are studying how CFAs may be adopted for certain categories of domestic proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intent is that the CFAs will allow for litigants, including businesses facing risks of insolvency or cash flow issues, to pursue meritorious claims which they may not otherwise have been able to pursue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, Sir, let me touch on some areas of family and civil justice which Members have spoken about.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about protections for certain vulnerable groups against family violence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have amended POHA, the CPC and the Penal Code to introduce a number of measures over the past few years, to tackle family violence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include introducing new offences and enhanced penalties to deter the abuse of: (a) persons with whom the offender was in an intimate or close relationship, such as members of the same household; (b) children under 14 years old; (c) persons who are substantially unable to protect themselves from such abuse, neglect, or self-neglect, by reason of mental or physical infirmity, disability or incapacity; and (d) foreign domestic workers – where the offender is the employer, member of the employer's household or the employment agent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have made offences committed against vulnerable victims arrestable; and we have simplified the application process for Personal Protection Orders (PPOs) and the Expedited Orders (EOs), in the form that I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: An Inter-Agency Task Force on Family Violence, led by MSF and MHA, was also set up in February 2020 to look into further strengthening protections.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That Task Force will submit its recommendations on how we can better prevent and deal with incidents of family violence in due course.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Zhulkarnian had asked if we were considering replacing the definition of "family violence" under the Women's Charter to cover groups such as "intimate partners" and those in "close relationships".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We should highlight that non-family members who suffer abuse are protected under the Penal Code and POHA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay raised some questions in relation to the Employment Claims Tribunal, or ECT.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Tay has suggested that for insolvent companies, MOM can advance money first to the worker and thereafter stand in his place as a preferred creditor.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I understand that MOM has looked at this proposal before.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It recognises that advancing money in such situations may provide relief to the worker in the immediate short term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, at the same time, it also distorts the market and may also inadvertently create a larger problem of a viable company defaulting or owing the salaries, when knowing that workers might then obtain such payments from Government funds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This may lead to a bigger systemic problem in the longer term.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Workers who are unable to recover unpaid salaries may also tap into the Short-term Relief Fund, or STRF and the Migrant Workers' Assistance Fund, or MWAF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those details, I will not go into, but, if Members have questions on them, either myself or MOM officers can assist.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Tay also mentioned the need to publish ECT judgments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, the judgments or grounds of decision may be made available to the public upon request.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In assessing requests, the ECT will consider factors such as whether these judgments when published will assist in future cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This practice is consistent with applications for judgments and grounds of decisions in the State Courts, including other tribunals such as the Small Claims Tribunals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MOM will make applications to the ECT to publish grounds of decision, when these would help to clarify common misunderstandings about common employment laws or increase awareness of employment obligations and rights.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These would then become useful references and precedents to the employers, employees and to mediators of subsequent cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I should add that the State Courts would also, on top of this, consider publishing selected ECT grounds of decision on an anonymised basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And second, the steps that we take to continue to enhance and strengthen Singapore as a leading international legal and dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Pillai mentioned, we rolled out a series of urgent measures in 2020 to support citizens and businesses in a very difficult time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These initiatives illustrate how my Ministry has helped Singaporeans ride out the impact of the COVID-19 storm, and emerge stronger together.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The temporary relief from contractual obligations, and rental relief framework provided much needed breathing space to businesses and individuals alike and promoted a fair sharing of obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Simplified Insolvency Programme, or SIP, and the Re-Align Framework, the two most recent ones in the measures, both aim to help the economy as a whole, pivot and emerge stronger from the crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Re-Align Framework allows eligible MSCs to renegotiate selected types of contracts with their counterparties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also received feedback that the introduction of the Framework in itself has promoted dialogues and discussions between parties to discuss constructive ways that they can themselves, without the help of assessors, forged forward with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many have successfully renegotiated their agreements without needing to even serve a notice under the Framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It really would not have been possible, without such a strong partnerships between the different sectors of the legal industry working hand-in-hand with many other agencies in Government and also with the private sector, especially the commercial businesses and chambers, all of whom have come together with suggestions or thoughts to make the legislation as wide-ranging and as efficient as possible in its implementation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked about smaller landlords – especially retirees – who do face genuine hardship in meeting their obligations under the framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not for every tenant, it is only for tenants who have themselves seen such a drop in their revenue.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MAS has also worked with the banks and finance companies to allow affected individual and SME landlords to defer their property loan repayments last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SMEs could defer their principal repayments, while individual landlords could defer both interest and principal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Eligible landlords who continue to experience cashflow difficulties this year can apply to their lenders for temporary reduced instalment plans, or work out alternative arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked if we intend to introduce any new measures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will make adjustments as may be necessary, and we will not shy away from introducing further measures should there be a need to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Pillai also suggested having a framework legislation that can be deployed quickly at the next crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We understand Mr Pillai's suggestion and I think the intent behind it is good to make it quick, flexible and easy to understand and implement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But at the same time, each crisis is different and its impact on aspects of business, which parts of the economy, how it might be felt, might be different with each crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: COVID-19 hit many businesses and sectors especially hard, particularly travel and conference sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The measures, I should emphasise, that we have put in place over the course of last year have been extraordinary, designed to meet an extraordinary crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The next one may well differ in its scope and scale.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We did not intervene in previous crises, for example, in SARS in 2003.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we must be careful and circumspect before intervening in private arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A framework legislation, whilst well-intentioned, might not be sufficiently nuanced itself and targeted to meet the unique challenges of the next crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our experience in responding swiftly to COVID-19 will nevertheless help to shape and sharpen our responses, moving forward.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, our system of governance allows us to move fast, be nimble and act quickly, for the benefit of Singaporeans, as we have demonstrated in the course of last year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We do have every confidence that should there be a need to in subsequent years – touch wood, that there will be no other such crisis – we will be able to respond in similar fashion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, there are some areas that we are looking at introducing more lasting changes which will take into account the lessons that we have learnt from the pandemic, drawing a leaf out of Mr Pillai's suggestion.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has been working with the Courts to drive the digital transformation of the litigation process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated the shift towards non-traditional modes of hearing, where both litigants and counsel may not be present before the judge in the same physical location at the same time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These may include conducting hearings through video-link and also based on documents filed by parties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The temporary measures under the COVID-19 Act have been positively received by court users and also, I understand, members of the Bar.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will build on these successes and facilitate the technological transformation of our court system and expand the existing scope of non-traditional modes of hearing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will, of course, also be subject – as Mr Pillai will understand – to appropriate safeguards to ensure that the propriety of the hearing, integrity and fairness, which are ultimately of paramount considerations, will be upheld.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes will help the Courts to improve the efficiency and accessibility of court processes, and also lower the cost of dispute-resolution for litigants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, Sir, strengthening Singapore as a leading international legal and dispute resolution hub remains high on the priority.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has been investing heavily in this, over the past decade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will to continue to push hard to enhance our value proposition, so that parties will find it attractive to procure legal services from Singapore-based firms, and to use Singapore as a trusted venue to resolve their disputes, even if the underlying transaction might have nothing to do with Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This creates economic value and good work for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we continue to take our standing on the international stage and international cooperation very seriously, to burnish our reputation as a reliable and trustworthy jurisdiction, that is a responsible actor on the global stage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore is the first and only other country to have such an arrangement with ITLOS.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Model Agreement reaffirms Singapore’s commitment to the international rule of law, on the peaceful settlement of disputes, and it is itself an endorsement of Singapore as a neutral venue for the effective settlement of international disputes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are pursuing a number of other efforts in the area of international civil cooperation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example, as Mr Pillai is well aware of, is the Apostille Convention, which Mr Pillai has brought up on several occasions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This facilitates cross-border recognition and use of public documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have begun consultations with stakeholders, including on the practicalities, the actual practical steps in implementing the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will update Mr Pillai when we have reached a landing on this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we continue to position Singapore as a thought leader on international rule of law matters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The key effort in this regard relates to the Singapore Convention on Mediation, as Mr Sitoh Yih Pin has highlighted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Members would recall, this is the first UN Convention bearing Singapore’s name.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving forward, we will continue to offer technical assistance on the Convention to other countries and promote its ratification, and maintain our position as a thought leader in this area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, we continue to strengthen our status as a leading international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh asked how we can continue to promote Singapore despite the restrictions because of COVID-19.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The pandemic has certainly affected the normal operations of our dispute resolution institutions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But they have responded swiftly, adapted and also enhanced their own technology offerings to better adapt to the evolving situation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) and Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) have made provisions for online arbitrations and mediations for parties almost immediately.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Maxwell Chambers pivoted from providing physical hearing spaces and facilities to offering parties integrated and seamless virtual and hybrid alternative dispute resolution (ADR) hearing services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It also collaborated with other hearing centres in the region to facilitate ADR hearings for international parties who may be located in different parts of the region, different venues physically.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to strengthen partnerships with key stakeholders and support these dispute resolution institutions in building up their international networks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, these institutions have continued to expand their global presence and partnerships, in some ways taking advantage of the COVID-19 period to build their future resources and to look at expanding their footprints.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It entered into collaboration with partner dispute resolution institutions and universities in key markets such as China, Japan and Thailand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIMC was also active in extending its international footprint, and forging closer collaborations with partners overseas, including with Japan and China.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is to establish a working group to study the feasibility of co-developing a dispute resolution mechanism between Singapore and China, and to see how Singapore can play a role in resolving disputes involving China and the countries along the Belt and Road initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Other than strengthening our international partnerships, we also amended the International Arbitration Act to further enhance our legal framework for international arbitration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has borne fruit with both SIAC and SIMC, achieving record caseloads in 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Going forward, we will continue to build on our strengths, what we have achieved so far, expand our international partnerships for global presence, and implement other legislative changes to keep our dispute resolution services and offerings vibrant, competitive and moving with the times.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are currently working on extending the existing third-party funding framework to domestic arbitration and also certain prescribed proceedings before the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I mentioned earlier, we are also working on introducing a framework for CFAs for the same categories of proceedings covered by the third-party funding framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes will serve to meet the demand for alternative funding arrangements by commercial litigants.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We envisage that it will also bring in more work for our lawyers, and level the playing field for them vis-à-vis foreign lawyers, who have already been able to offer such arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have been continuing to develop Singapore’s intellectual property (IP) eco-system, to maintain our top ranked IP regime and establish Singapore as a global hub for IP and intangible assets (IA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we launched the SG IP Fast programme in 2020, to fast track the registration of patents, and related trademarks and registered designs in Singapore, to cut the processing time for businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Member will appreciate, time is efficiency and is profitability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, our IP efforts have been focused on cutting down the amount of time needed for these processes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, to support enterprise growth through IP and IA, we have partnered SGX to launch the Intangible Disclosure Evaluation and Audit Scheme or IDEAS to encourage companies to undergo IA evaluations and promote a more robust IA disclosure regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
